builder_plan.scenario: Your self-hosted model spends too long generating answers token by token.
builder_plan.change: Check whether a compatible draft model and serving integration exist before renting compute.
builder_plan.baseline: The same target with speculation off, then your existing drafter if you have one.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Accepted draft length, tokens per second, tail latency, output quality, and total GPU cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: LEGOSpec: A Composable and Efficient Framework for Speculative Draft Design and Training
summary: LEGOSpec replaces monolithic speculative-draft recipes (EAGLE-style fixed designs trained under mismatched conditions) with a composable Context/Backbone/Proposal/Objective framework, and its DFlux configuration replaces the strongest existing baseline draft. The cost is a draft-training pipeline (supervision data from the target model, plus training compute that the framework makes up to 79% more efficient), additional inference memory for the draft, and integration complexity in the serving stack; adoption via the draft adds negligible per-token latency only when acceptance is high. It can fail when the workload shifts (backbone choice is context- and memory-dependent, so a draft tuned for short contexts underperforms on long ones), when the target model differs from the Qwen/Gemma families evaluated, or when proposal latency outweighs acceptance gains at small batch sizes.
rationale: Speculative decoding is directly deployable on a single 24 GB GPU for inference speedup, but the paper's gains depend on training a custom draft matched to the reader's model and workload, so the balanced DFlux configuration should be validated on the reader's own traffic before production adoption.
technique: Composable speculative draft design and training

claims.statement: LEGOSpec replaces monolithic speculative-draft recipes (EAGLE-style fixed designs trained under mismatched conditions) with a composable Context/Backbone/Proposal/Objective framework, and its DFlux configuration replaces the strongest existing baseline draft. The cost is a draft-training pipeline (supervision data from the target model, plus training compute that the framework makes up to 79% more efficient), additional inference memory for the draft, and integration complexity in the serving stack; adoption via the draft adds negligible per-token latency only when acceptance is high. It can fail when the workload shifts (backbone choice is context- and memory-dependent, so a draft tuned for short contexts underperforms on long ones), when the target model differs from the Qwen/Gemma families evaluated, or when proposal latency outweighs acceptance gains at small batch sizes.

DFlux improves acceptance length over the strongest baseline by up to 13.7% on regular benchmarks and 34.7% on long-context workloads; LEGOSpec's scheduling and asynchronous execution increase draft training throughput by up to 79% (1.79x) and accelerate offline supervision preparation by up to 3.11x over SpecForge.
